items.title: Macroscopic and microscopic entropy quantities
items.design_state: Draft carrier authored; prerequisites and independent review pending.
items.statement:
Fix a material constitution $c$ and its equilibrium state domain $D_c$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. The adopted macroscopic entropy is the finite-valued state function $S_c:D_c\to\mathbb R$ of [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]: for every $x\in D_c$, $S_c(x)$ is a finite real value measured in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ under [[def-td-si-quantities]]. Its argument is an equilibrium macrostate. The definition does not assign $S_c$ to an arbitrary nonequilibrium configuration or to a microscopic trajectory.

For a finite microstate model $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ of [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]], $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty and $\epsilon:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ assigns a finite numerical energy. The model's physical energy is $E(x)=\epsilon(x)\,\mathrm J$ for $x\in\Omega$, with its zero and any retained internal offsets fixed by the declared material model. By [[def-finite-cardinality]], $N:=|\Omega|$ is the unique natural number equinumerous with $\Omega$, and $N\ge1$. Choose an enumeration $\Omega=\{\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_N\}$. A chosen coarse-graining is a finite label set $\mathcal M$ and a function $\pi:\Omega\to\mathcal M$ ([[def-function]]). For $m\in\mathcal M$, let $M_m=\{x\in\Omega:\pi(x)=m\}\subseteq\Omega$ ([[def-subset-and-proper-subset]]). Each $M_m$ is finite: choose a bijection $b:N\to\Omega$ and set $J_m=b^{-1}(M_m)\subseteq N$. Induction on $n$ ([[thm-induction-principle]]) proves every subset $J\subseteq n$ finite. For $n=0$, $J=\varnothing$; for $n=\sigma(k)$, if $k\notin J$, then $J\subseteq k$; if $k\in J$, the set $J_0:=\{j\in J:j\ne k\}\subseteq k$ is finite by induction, say via a bijection $f:n_0\to J_0$, and extending $f$ by $f(n_0)=k$ gives a bijection $\sigma(n_0)\to J$. Thus $J_m$ is finite, and the restriction $b|_{J_m}:J_m\to M_m$ is a bijection. By [[def-finite-cardinality]], $N_m:=|M_m|$ is therefore defined. Only labels with $N_m\ge1$ are admitted here. The Boltzmann macrocell entropy of this specified coarse-graining is

$$S_{\mathrm B}(m):=k_{\mathrm B}\log N_m.$$

Under this enumeration, a probability vector $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_N)$ assigns probability $p_i$ to microstate $\omega_i$, where $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_{i=1}^N p_i=1$. Define its Gibbs–Shannon entropy by

$$S_{\mathrm G}(p):=-k_{\mathrm B}\sum_{i=1}^N p_i\log p_i,$$

with the summand $p_i\log p_i$ defined to be $0$ when $p_i=0$. Both expressions have units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, because their logarithms are dimensionless and $k_{\mathrm B}$ has those units. The finite sum and logarithm have the meanings of [[def-finite-sum]] and [[def-natural-logarithm]].

For a density operator $\rho$ in the declared finite-dimensional sector class of [[def-nrqm-many-body-framework-entropy-and-free-energy]], its von Neumann physical entropy is $S_{\mathrm{vN}}(\rho)=k_{\mathrm B}s(\rho)$, with $s(\rho)$ the dimensionless entropy defined there. That supplier defines no such quantity for its infinite-dimensional spatial sectors.

These are distinct definitions on different domains: $S_c$ acts on an equilibrium macrostate, $S_{\mathrm B}$ on a chosen macrocell, $S_{\mathrm G}$ on a specified probability vector, and $S_{\mathrm{vN}}$ on a finite-sector density operator. A numerical equality among them requires an additional, explicit identification of model, coarse-graining, preparation and applicable limit. This item supplies no such identification and adopts no canonical or microcanonical sampling rule.

items.title: Evidence records for irreversible and transport claims
items.design_state: Draft carrier authored; prerequisites and independent review pending.
items.statement:
**Evidence record.**

An empirical claim in a later item must identify the source report and exact locator, the material and sample, apparatus and geometry, boundary and control conditions, operational definitions of measured quantities, calibration, sampling procedure, and the source's reported uncertainty and systematic limitations. Preserve the units, resolution, sample size, and selection conditions actually given by the source. If the source omits one of these details, record the omission and limit the claim; do not supply a plausible value or precision.

Keep four records separate: source-reported observations; derived estimates from those observations; model predictions under stated assumptions; and statistical comparisons between estimates and predictions. State the sampling and measurement model and the inference method when a statistical conclusion is made. Agreement supports the specified model-and-apparatus combination; it does not prove a postulate. Evidence belongs in an experiment item or a nonlogical evidence relation unless a theorem actually assumes a qualified empirical result, in which case that qualification must be carried as an empirical premise.

The source treatments cited here discuss modelled fluctuations and transport. Their illustrative numerical values are not measurements made by this library. No experiment item or observation is supplied by this remark.

items.title: Hypotheses for microscopic fluctuation claims
items.design_state: Draft carrier authored; prerequisites and independent review pending.
items.statement:
**Scope.**

The adopted [[post-td-macroscopic-second-law]] compares the total macroscopic entropies of specified equilibrium endpoints of an admitted isolated process record. It assigns no entropy function to nonequilibrium intermediate configurations and does not assert that every microscopic realization has nonnegative entropy change. The macrostate and finite-model quantities remain distinct as defined in [[def-td-macro-versus-micro-entropy-claim]].

A stochastic fluctuation claim needs its own state space or path space, probability law, preparation, driving protocol, time interval, measured or modelled random variable, and averaging convention. A trajectory observable has the units stated by its model (for physical entropy production, $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$; for dimensionless entropy production, no units). If a trajectory variable is called entropy production, define it and state the hypotheses of the relation being used, including the forward and reverse protocols and the support and integrability conditions needed for the stated averages. Positivity of an ensemble mean does not imply positivity in every realization.

For a precise model, let $X$ be a specified set of states and let $\tau>0$ seconds. The time domain $[0,\tau]$ is the closed interval of [[def-interval]]. Let $\Gamma$ be a specified set of allowed sample paths $\gamma:[0,\tau]\to X$, where each $\gamma$ is a function in the sense of [[def-function]]. Any further path regularity or admissibility conditions are part of that model; none is imposed universally here. Equip $\Gamma$ with an event $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal F$ and choose a probability measure $P$ on $(\Gamma,\mathcal F)$. A trajectory observable is a measurable map $\Sigma:(\Gamma,\mathcal F)\to(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$, where $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra; if it represents physical entropy production, the model assigns its values units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, while a dimensionless entropy production has no units. When $\Sigma$ is $P$-integrable, meaning $\int_\Gamma |\Sigma|\,dP<\infty$, its expectation is the integral $\mathbb E_P[\Sigma]:=\int_\Gamma\Sigma\,dP$ by [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. A driving protocol is a declared control map $\lambda:[0,\tau]\to\Lambda$, with its parameter space $\Lambda$, regularity and endpoint controls specified by the model; $\lambda$ is also a function as in [[def-function]]. Any reverse-protocol comparison needs its own path measure and support conditions.

The fluctuation–dissipation theorem discussed in the cited treatments relates equilibrium fluctuations to a specified linear response of a coupled model. It is distinct from a trajectory fluctuation relation and does not by itself prove the macroscopic second-law postulate. No universal microscopic fluctuation formula or trajectory-wise entropy inequality is asserted here.

items.title: Scope of a local-equilibrium continuum branch
items.design_state: Draft carrier authored; prerequisites and independent review pending.
items.statement:
**Scope and objects.**

For a declared continuum model, let $m\in\mathbb N$ with $m\ge1$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]) and let $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open in the metric topology induced by the Euclidean norm ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-metric-topology]], [[def-subset-and-proper-subset]]). Its spatial coordinates are in metres. In the conventional physical display $\mathbf x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, $x_i$ denotes the function coordinate at index $i-1$ of the library's $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Let $I=(t_0,t_1)\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of time ([[def-interval]]) with coordinates in seconds. A field is a function on the stated space-time domain, with its domain and codomain shown, as in [[def-function]]. The model chooses a local-state parameter set $\mathcal Z\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and a field $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_m):\mathcal O\times I\to\mathcal Z$ whose component functions have continuous first partial derivatives in the three spatial coordinates and time; the partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Each $z_j$ is the dimensionless numerical value of its local quantity divided by its model-declared reference unit $u_j$; the model specifies $u_j$ and the physical meaning of each component. In particular, if temperature is the component $z_{j_T}$, the model declares that index and reads $T(\mathbf x,t)=(1\,\mathrm K)z_{j_T}(\mathbf x,t)$, so $T:\mathcal O\times I\to(0,\infty)$ has units kelvins. If the model includes mass density and fluid velocity, their types are $\rho:\mathcal O\times I\to[0,\infty)$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ and $\mathbf u:\mathcal O\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; these fields may also be required to have continuous first partial derivatives. Each model must specify its remaining coordinates and equation of state; $\mathcal Z$ is not universal.

A **local-equilibrium approximation** is a model-declared map $q:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal E_{\mathrm{eq}}$, where $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the model's set of local equilibrium constitutive states, together with the assumption that the state assigned at $(\mathbf x,t)$ is $q(z(\mathbf x,t))$. A model using finite coarse-grained cells must separately specify its cell partition and the map from cells to local parameters; this remark adopts no such partition. A kinetic model may declare a mean free path $\ell>0\,\mathrm m$ from its intercollision-distance law, a characteristic field-variation length $L>0\,\mathrm m$, a collision-relaxation time $\tau_{\mathrm c}>0\,\mathrm s$, and a protocol-variation time $\tau_{\mathrm m}>0\,\mathrm s$. The model must give the mathematical construction of each scale (including any distribution and finite-mean condition when it uses an expectation) and its criterion for scale separation. Such a model may require $\ell/L\ll1$ and $\tau_{\mathrm c}/\tau_{\mathrm m}\ll1$; the meaning of $\ll1$ is set by that model and has no universal numerical threshold. Where a kinetic model has a distribution $f$ on a declared phase space and a local-equilibrium distribution $f_0(z)$, write its deviation as $\delta f:=f-f_0(z)$; $f$, $f_0$ and their domains are supplied by that model, and the local-equilibrium distribution alone need not solve the kinetic evolution equation.

Nonconstant fields $T(\mathbf x,t)$, $\rho(\mathbf x,t)$, or $\mathbf u(\mathbf x,t)$ are permitted in this continuum model and do not describe global equilibrium. Initial data, boundary conditions, conservation equations, constitutive assumptions and their empirical scope must be supplied before any time evolution or transport conclusion is claimed.

items.title: Unitary invariance of finite-sector quantum entropy
items.design_state: Draft carrier authored; prerequisites and independent review pending.
items.statement:
Adopt exactly the state, observable, autonomous-dynamics and canonical-ensemble assumptions, readings, finite-dimensional sector class, and normalized canonical preparation of [[pthm-nrqm-many-body-unitary-evolution-preserves-entropy]]. The sector $\mathfrak H_N^\sigma$ and its self-adjoint energy operator $H_N^\sigma$ are those of [[def-nrqm-many-body-framework-declared-fixed-n-model]]. Model time $t$ is in seconds, $H_N^\sigma$ is in joules, and $\hbar=h/(2\pi)$ is the reduced Planck constant in $\mathrm{J\,s}$, as in [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. The evolution definition [[def-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-framework-evolution]] gives $U(t)=\exp(-itH_N^\sigma/\hbar)$ and $\rho(t)=U(t)\rho(0)U(t)^*$. Both the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice are assumed ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Define $S_{\mathrm{vN}}(\rho)=k_{\mathrm B}s(\rho)$ as in [[def-nrqm-many-body-framework-entropy-and-free-energy]]. Then, for every declared sector preparation $\rho(0)$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$:

1. $S_{\mathrm{vN}}(\rho(t))=S_{\mathrm{vN}}(\rho(0))$;
2. the adopted canonical preparation is stationary; and
3. a preparation different from the canonical one is never mapped to it by this unitary flow.

These are statements about the exact closed finite-sector model. They do not identify $S_{\mathrm{vN}}$ with the macroscopic equilibrium entropy $S_c$ of [[def-td-macro-versus-micro-entropy-claim]], derive the canonical preparation, or establish bath relaxation or thermalization.

I. Burmistrov and A. Lunkin, Lecture Notes on Statistical Mechanics (10 January 2023), §§1.1.1–1.1.3, printed pp. 12–14

items.title: Scope of transport constitutive laws
items.design_state: Draft carrier authored; prerequisites and independent review pending.
items.statement:
**Scope.**

Use the fields and local-equilibrium regime of [[rem-td-local-equilibrium-branch]]. For this constitutive relation, assume $T$ has continuous first spatial partial derivatives, defined as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and write

$\nabla T:=(\partial_{x_1}T,\partial_{x_2}T,\partial_{x_3}T)\in\mathbb R^3.$

Here the physical coordinate indices $i=1,2,3$ correspond to function indices $i-1$ in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

The components of $\nabla T$ have units $\mathrm{K\,m^{-1}}$.

Matrices are elements of $M_{3\times3}(\mathbb R)$ as in [[def-matrix-space]]. In the physical one-based display, $K_{ij}$ denotes the library matrix entry with indices $(i-1,j-1)$, and $v_i$ denotes vector coordinate $i-1$, for $i,j=1,2,3$. The action is $(Kv)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^3K_{ij}v_j$; $I_3$ is the matrix with entries $1$ on the diagonal and $0$ off it as in [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. A Fourier heat-transport model may postulate

$$\mathbf j_Q(\mathbf x,t)=-K(\mathbf x,t)\nabla T(\mathbf x,t),$$

where $\mathbf j_Q:\mathcal O\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is a continuous heat-energy flux field in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ and $K:\mathcal O\times I\to M_{3\times3}(\mathbb R)$ is a declared conductivity tensor field with entries in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. In an isotropic model $K(\mathbf x,t)=\kappa(\mathbf x,t)I_3$, where $\kappa:\mathcal O\times I\to[0,\infty)$ is the declared scalar conductivity field. A diffusion model may separately postulate $\mathbf j_n=-D\nabla n$, where number density $n:\mathcal O\times I\to[0,\infty)$ is in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, number flux $\mathbf j_n:\mathcal O\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is in $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, and $D$ is either a scalar field $D:\mathcal O\times I\to\mathbb R$ or a matrix field $D:\mathcal O\times I\to M_{3\times3}(\mathbb R)$ with coefficient units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$; its regularity and positivity conditions are model data.

These are constitutive choices for specified material, geometry, regime, field regularity and boundary conditions. In a kinetic model with microscopic state space $\Xi$ and allowed collision transitions $\mathcal C\subseteq\Xi\times\Xi$, a collision invariant is a real-valued function $Q:\Xi\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $Q(\xi')=Q(\xi)$ for every $(\xi,\xi')\in\mathcal C$. If the model has a distribution $f$ on a declared phase space and a collision operator $C[f]$ giving the collision contribution to its evolution, a single-relaxation-time replacement may be $C_\tau[f]=-(f-f_0)/\tau$, with model-declared reference distribution $f_0$ and $\tau>0$. This replacement need not preserve collision invariants unless it is constrained to preserve their integrals against the model's state distribution. Different kinetic, linear-response and quantum transport models use different hypotheses and coefficient definitions; a coefficient derived in one is not thereby universal. No kinetic operator or reciprocity law is defined or asserted here. Microscopic calculations and measurements may determine or test coefficients for a specified model and material, but neither the equilibrium entropy postulates nor dimensional consistency alone determine them.

Any heat equation or transport conclusion additionally needs the relevant conservation balance, sources or work terms, constitutive relation, initial data and boundary conditions. No such evolution equation, Onsager relation, or transport coefficient is proved or adopted by this remark.

items.title: A macrocell count and a nonuniform microscopic distribution
items.design_state: Draft carrier authored; prerequisites and independent review pending.
items.statement: Let $\Omega=\{\omega_1,\omega_2\}$, put both states in one macrocell $M_m=\Omega$, and assign $p_1=1,\ p_2=0$. The model is deliberately nonuniform. It shows that the macrocell-count definition and the Gibbs–Shannon definition can take different values on separately specified inputs.
items.physical_scope: A stipulated two-microstate finite model with a nonuniform probability vector; it is not an equilibrium preparation, measurement or empirical claim.

items.title: Positive ensemble mean with a negative realization
items.design_state: Draft carrier authored; prerequisites and independent review pending.
items.statement:
Let $\Omega=\{\omega_+,\omega_-\}$ with weights $w(\omega_+)=3/4$ and $w(\omega_-)=1/4$. Both weights are nonnegative and sum to $1$, so $(\Omega,w)$ is a finite probability space as defined in [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]. For every event $A\subseteq\Omega$, write $P(A)=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega)$ for its event probability. Let $Y:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be given by $Y(\omega_+)=2a$ and $Y(\omega_-)=-2a$, where $a>0$ and the values are numerical values in the unit $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. By [[def-finite-real-random-variable-and-distribution]], $Y$ is a finite-valued real random variable on this finite probability space, so its expectation is a finite sum. The label $Y$ is only an illustrative entropy-valued variable; this example adopts no physical path law.

This arithmetic example illustrates the distinction in [[rem-td-fluctuation-model-hypotheses]].
items.physical_scope: A two-outcome probability model for an illustrative entropy-valued random variable; it is not a specified physical fluctuation law or reported observation.

items.title: A nonconstant local-equilibrium temperature field
items.design_state: Draft carrier authored; prerequisites and independent review pending.
items.statement:
Use the one-coordinate convention of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] explicitly: $\iota:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^1$ sends $a$ to the function on $\{0\}$ with value $\iota(a)(0)=a$, and the inverse takes the coordinate at index zero. In every scalar display below, a one-coordinate parameter or field is written through this bijection. Thus $\mathcal Z$ means $\iota((0,\infty))$, the scalar formula for $z$ denotes its $\iota$ image, $C(e,y)=e$ means $C(e,y)=\iota(e)$, $c(a)=a$ is the identity on $\mathcal Z$, and $q(\iota(a))=(a,0)$; temperature and inequalities use the scalar coordinate $a$. This is a notation convention, not a set-theoretic identity between a real and a function.

Take $\mathcal O=(0,L)^3$ in metre coordinates and $I=(0,\tau)$ in second coordinates, with $L>0\,\mathrm m$ and $\tau>0\,\mathrm s$. Choose $\Theta_0>0\,\mathrm K$ and dimensionless $0<\alpha<1$. Instantiate $m=1$ and the local-state parameter set $\mathcal Z=(0,\infty)\subseteq\mathbb R^1$, and define its one-coordinate field $z:\mathcal O\times I\to\mathcal Z$ by

$$z(\mathbf x,t)=\frac{\Theta_0}{1\,\mathrm K}\left(1+\alpha\frac{x_1}{L}\right),\qquad T(\mathbf x,t)=(1\,\mathrm K)z(\mathbf x,t)=\Theta_0\left(1+\alpha\frac{x_1}{L}\right).$$

For the homogeneous comparison cell, supply $\mathcal X=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ with states $(e,y)$, physical energy $(1\,\mathrm J)e$, and numerical entropy $s(e,y)=\ln e-y^2$, where $\ln:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the natural logarithm of [[def-natural-logarithm]] and physical entropy is $(1\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}})s(e,y)$. The coordinate $y$ is dimensionless. Set $r=1$, $C(e,y)=e$, $c(a)=a$, and $B_a=\mathcal X$ for every $a\in\mathcal Z$, so the fixed-energy admissible set is $A_a=\{(a,y):y\in\mathbb R\}$. Its entropy-maximizing set is $E_a=\{(a,0)\}$. Define $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{eq}}=\bigcup_{a>0}E_a$ and supply $q(a)=(a,0)$; assign this comparison state temperature $(1\,\mathrm K)a$. Stipulate the local-equilibrium approximation with this map, so the local constitutive state at $(\mathbf x,t)$ is $q(z(\mathbf x,t))$. The field is static and nonconstant; this stipulation is a model assumption, not an assertion that a physical sample realizes the profile.
items.physical_scope: A stipulated static local-equilibrium field on an open cube; no global equilibrium, transport law or observation is asserted.

items.title: Different Fourier coefficients give different model fluxes
items.design_state: Draft carrier authored; prerequisites and independent review pending.
items.statement: On $\mathcal O=(0,L)^3$ in metre coordinates and $I=(0,\tau)$ in second coordinates, with $L>0\,\mathrm m$ and $\tau>0\,\mathrm s$, prescribe $T(\mathbf x,t)=T_0+\Delta T\,x_1/L$, where $T_0>0\,\mathrm K$ and $\Delta T>0\,\mathrm K$. In the chosen Cartesian coordinates, define $\mathbf e_1:=(1,0,0)\in\mathbb R^3$. Compare two isotropic model choices $\kappa_1,\kappa_2>0$, $\kappa_1\ne\kappa_2$, each using $\mathbf j_Q=-\kappa_i\nabla T$. The coefficients have units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.
items.physical_scope: Comparison of two stipulated isotropic Fourier models on the same temperature profile; no material measurement or universal constitutive law is asserted.
